documentation.range:
Macaca fascicularis is widely distributed across South and Southeast Asia (Fooden 1995, Gumert 2011). Throughout this large range, the species is patchy in occurrence and not continuously distributed (Eudey 2008, Gamalo et al. 2024, Koch Liston et al. 2024). In South Asia, the species used to occur in Bangladesh, though it is now considered extinct there (Gamalo et al. 2024; Koch Liston et al. 2024) and only remains in the Nicobar Islands. In Southeast Asia, they occur in the northern coastal region of Rakhine (Myanmar), spreading south through the coastal lowlands of Myanmar, and east through Thailand, most of Cambodia, the southeastern tip of Lao PDR, and southern Viet Nam (Fooden 1995). M. fascicularis extends south through the Thai-Malay peninsula, into the Indonesian islands, including Borneo, and throughout the islands of the Philippines. Long-tailed Macaques also occur on numerous islands throughout Southeast Asia (Fooden 1995).

The following subspecies of Macaca fascicularis are currently recognized:
  1. The common subspecies, Macaca fascicularis fascicularis, occupies much of this range, except for the western-most fringe around Myanmar (which is inhabited by M. f. aurea) and seven small islands or archipelagos, inhabited by the other eight subspecies listed below. Macaca fascicularis fascicularis is listed as Endangered (Hansen et al. 2022c).
  2. Macaca fascicularis atriceps occurs on Khram Yai Island, off the southeastern coast of Thailand (Groves 2001) and is listed as Vulnerable (Ang et al. 2022).
  3. Macaca fascicularis aurea occurs within mainland and insular Myanmar and some southern parts of central Thailand and northwestern parts of southern Thailand (San and Hamada 2011, Gumert et al. 2014) and is listed as Vulnerable (Gumert et al. 2022).
  4. Macaca fascicularis condorensis occurs on Con Son and Hon Ba Islands, off the coast of southern Viet Nam (Groves 2001) and is listed as Endangered (Quyet and Hansen 2022).
  5. Macaca fascicularis fusca occurs on Simeulue Island, off the northwestern coast of Sumatra, Indonesia (Groves 2001) and is listed as Critically Endangered (Amey et al. 2022a).
  6. Macaca fascicularis karimondjawae occurs on Karimunjawa and Kemujan Islands, Java Sea, Indonesia (Groves 2001) and is listed as Critically Endangered (Kristiawan et al. 2022).
  7. Macaca fascicularis lasiae occurs on Lasia Island, off the northwestern coast of Sumatra, Indonesia (Groves 2001) and is listed as Critically Endangered (Amey et al. 2022b).
  8. Macaca fascicularis tua occurs on Maratua Island, east of Borneo, Indonesia (Groves 2001) and is listed as Critically Endangered (Nuryati et al. 2022).
  9. Macaca fascicularis umbrosa occurs on Nicobar Islands of India, which include Little Nicobar, Great Nicobar and Katchall Islands, (Umapathy et al. 2003) and is listed as Vulnerable (Ramakrishna et al. 2022).
There are also cases of humans moving this species beyond its original range. The known cases are an island off the coast of Sulawesi (Froehlich et al. 2003), West Papua (Kemp and Burnett 2007), Mauritius, Hong Kong (Southwick and Southwick 1983), and Palau (Poirier and Smith 1974). Noting, however, that they are now extirpated from Hong Kong (Karthi Martelli pers. comm. 2022) and undergoing population control with the aim of extirpation in West Papua (Kemp and Burnett 2004).
documentation.population:
The Long-tailed Macaque (Macaca fascicularis) is inferred to have undergone a 50% population decline over the past three generations (1995 – 2022; ~ 30 years) due to habitat loss and high levels of exploitation, and is therefore assessed as Endangered under criterion A2cd. In addition, as the threats facing the species and levels of exploitation have not been mitigated and continues at a similar pace, it is suspected that the species will continue to experience a population decline at a rate of 50% over the coming three generations (30 years), and is therefore also assessed as Endangered under criterion A3cd. A summary of population data, which has informed this assessment, is set out below. In addition, data regarding the threats facing the species are set out elsewhere in this assessment.

Past population size estimates: Please see Table 1, Supplementary Information. In 1995, Fooden (1995, p. 54) – based on past population assessments (Mackinnon 1986, Mackinnon and Mackinnon 1987) – estimated the entire M. fascicularis population to have been around 5 million in the 1980s. One decade later, Fooden (2006, p. 5) indirectly estimated the entire population to have declined to about 3 million by 2006. Although this was an indirect population estimate, these historical figures indicate a 40% decline in the species over approximately a two-generational (i.e., 20-year) time period from the mid-1980s to the mid-2000s. Given that removal and environmental impacts have increased (as noted elsewhere in this assessment), it is suspected that population declines have continued and even increased since the last assessment in 2006.

There are data that provide evidence that this species has undergone population declines (examples are set out here in narrative format and are also listed below in Table 1, Supplementary Information). For example:

1) Data from Keo Seima, Cambodia evidences an approximately 40% decline in Long-tailed Macaques between 2010-2022 (Agger 2022). If such a decline is extrapolated to 3 generations, it would correspond to over 70% decline.

2) As another example, Long-tailed Macaques in southern Sumatra, Indonesia may have also experienced a substantial decline in population size from 1995 to 2023 (Supriatna et al. 1996, Iqbal et al. 2024). In 1995, the population size in South Sumatra province was estimated at 1,925,000 individuals. In 2023, in Bengkulu, Jambi and Lampung provinces combined, the population size was estimated at 300,000 individuals. All provinces are located in southern Sumatra and equal in size (Bengkulu, Jambi and Lampung combined are only slightly larger than South Sumatra), combined with the level of habitat loss in the region (up to 50%) and the threats from hunting, it is possible to infer a population decline across southern Sumatra (Supriatna et al. 1996, Supriatna et al. 2017, Iqbal et al. 2024). It is important to note, however, that the methods used to calculate abundance in South Sumatra were not disclosed and seemed to be derived from direct sightings that were significantly lower (4,316 individuals).

3) In addition, there have been observed localised population declines, for example in: 1) areas where human provisioning has resulted in high densities of Long-tailed Macaques (leading to negative interactions between humans and macaques, resulting in culling and capturing events; Gamalo et al. 2024); and 2) areas where there have been local declines and even complete disappearances, such as Cambodia (Lee 2011, Agger 2022), Lao PDR (Gamalo et al. 2024), and Bangladesh (Gamalo et al. 2024).

4) Finally, a recent publication covering most of the range of the species indicates a large decline (up to 80%) in population size in comparison to Fooden’s estimate in 1995. However, as the methods differ, a direct comparison is not possible, yet the results are relevant in serving as a current baseline for the species’ population, which can enable rigorous monitoring going forward. Importantly, Koch Liston et al. (2024) report upper limit abundance and presumably overestimate the population size as the model is benchmarked against protected areas and areas with an abundance of data.
 
Population density estimates: Densities and detection rates seem to be decreasing and/or are low in some areas. Mean density reported by Fooden (1995) was 55 ind/km² for non-provisioned Long-tailed Macaque across habitats. For provisioned groups, Fooden (1995) referenced Wheatley (1989) of a density of 1,600 ind/km² in Bali. However, recent studies have reported mean densities ranging from 0.833 ind/km² in Keo Seima Wildlife Sanctuary in Cambodia (Nuttall et al. 2021) to 41.4 ind/km² in Baluran National Park, East Java (Hansen et al. 2019) for non-provisioned groups, and to 520 ind/km² in Pangandaran, West Java, Indonesia, (Vincent Nijman pers. obs. 2022) for provisioned groups. However, information is sparse and often anecdotal and collected using a variety of methods, including some with low levels of accuracy. A recent rapid survey of protected areas in Viet Nam revealed that the species is present in most national parks, but there were few groups and group sizes were low (10-40 ind) (Thu Huong Trinh pers. obs. 2022). In an area of Cambodia, the detection rate of Long-tailed Macaque by camera traps declined over just a one-year period (2013 – 2014; Suzuki et al. 2017).

Detection rates and effects of synanthropy: In Indonesian Borneo, camera traps failed to detect the species in Kutai National Park over the course of nine years, between 2011 and 2022 (Cheyne et al. 2025). Across the seven sites investigated by Cheyne et al., occupancy probability averaged to 0.28 — a remarkably low level, indicating an absence of M. fascicularis even in protected areas. These observations are not considered in the recent extrapolation of the Non-Detrimental Findings report for Indonesia (BRIN and KLHK, 2023), which estimates 105,187 individuals in all protected areas of the country. A rapid survey across 25 villages in Lao PDR, from May 2021 to June 2022, estimates no more than 600 individuals, including hybrids, in the country (Phiapalath 2023, Table 1). It should be noted that the synanthropic nature of the species has resulted in a trend of overestimation of their population sizes and a misinterpretation of abundance data (Kyes et al. 2011, Hansen et al. 2019, Holzner et al. 2025). It has also been noted that there has sometimes been a lack of a scientific approach to population size estimation (SSN 2012, 2015a, 2015b).

Range in population sizes: While nationwide and regional surveys generally point to a decline in Long-tailed Macaque populations (see Table 1, Supplementary Information), a commentary by Hilborn and Smith (2024) questioned this decline, referring to the species’ capacity for population growth. Some studies have reported localised population increases, particularly in urban or culturally protected areas. For instance, Brotcorne et al. (2015) observed an average annual increase of 11% in the Long-tailed Macaque population in Padangtegal, Bali, from 1986 to 2012. Under certain conditions, populations of Long-tailed Macaques may thrive, and this population in Bali is a good example of this, as it is heavily provisioned, well managed, and provided with medical care (Loudon et al. 2023). Furthermore, Karuppannan et al. (2014) suggested a 5% yearly growth rate in Kuala Lumpur, though this figure could not be verified. In Thailand, temple-dwelling populations of Long-tailed Macaques were found to have increased by 5- to 10-fold between 1992 and 2008 (Malaivijitnond and Hamada 2008), likely linked to the Buddhist practice of showing respect for all living beings. Macaques residing in temple areas are regularly fed by monks and pilgrims while protected from hunting and predators (Aggimarangsee and Brockelman 2005). Notably, these examples of localised population growth represent exceptions rather than the norm, as they are closely linked to human intervention, such as provisioning and protection, and do not reflect the broader status of the species in the wild.

A publication by Moore et al. (2023) argued that there had been an increase in Long-tailed Macaque density and abundance across mainland Southeast Asia, Sumatra, and Borneo. However, a commentary and reanalysis published in the same journal (Holzner et al. 2025) questions the conclusions and data analysis of this study. Holzner et al. highlight several issues in the analytical framework of Moore et al. (2023) and discusses the problems of data misinterpretation, in the context of synanthropic species like the Long-tailed Macaque. Moore et al. (2023) compared density and abundance between degraded and intact habitats, rather than assessing population trends over time. They reported a 520% higher density of Long-tailed Macaques in degraded habitats compared to more intact forests; however, this result is based on an error in data acquisition which, when corrected, would reverse the finding (i.e., indicating a higher density in intact habitats; Holzner et al. 2025).

Furthermore, a reanalysis of Moore et al. (2023)’s dataset on camera trap estimates from studies published between 1993 and 2021 (Moore et al. 2023, Tables S2 and S3) revealed that M. fascicularis was absent from 44% of habitats characterised by medium to high forest integrity (Holzner et al. 2025). Similar trends have been observed in a study by Cheyne et al. (2025), where camera traps failed to detect the species in Kutai National Park, Indonesian Borneo, over nine years (2011-2022). Across the seven sites investigated by Cheyne et al. (2025), occupancy probability averaged 0.28 – a remarkably low level, indicating an absence of M. fascicularis even in protected areas. This aligns with previous reports noting that the synanthropic nature of the species makes it prone to overestimation of population sizes when extrapolating local population sizes in anthropogenic landscapes to other areas (Kyes et al. 2011, Hansen et al. 2019).

It is also pertinent to note that the wide range of the species has never enabled a systematic population survey across its range or over time, which means that surveys were conducted by different individuals using different methods, with some methods being questionable. This makes a direct comparison difficult, and as you will see below, for example, Fooden estimated a total of 5 million Long-tailed Macaques in 1995 (Fooden 1995) and 3 million individuals in 2006 (Fooden 2006), however, the Cambodian government estimate the Cambodian population to be 3 million in 2009 in that country alone (CITES 2016), noting that there is no survey methodology provided by the Cambodian government, as it relates to this population estimate. However, recent research points to a large decline in Cambodia when compared to all historical results on Long-tailed Macaque population sizes. If the estimate of Cambodia in 2009 (CITES 2016) was appropriate, this would infer a fluctuation in the population size over the past three generations with a increase between 1995 and 2009, when compared to Fooden's estimates (Fooden 1995, 2006) and inferring a large decline (up to more than 90%) since 2009, when compared to the estimate of Koch-Liston et al. (2024) and local estimates (see e.g. Agger 2022).

For this reason, and for this assessment, we sought expert advice from habitat-country researchers, especially through a threat analysis conducted during the recent Population Viability Analysis (PVA) by the IUCN SSC Conservation Planning Specialist Group (see below for more information on this analysis).
 
Threat analysis workshop: In 2023, the IUCN Conservation Planning Specialist Group started a Population Viability Analysis process, which included a threat analysis workshop seeking to elicit qualitative estimates of levels of exploitation from habitat-country experts (Valle 2024) The working group identified that biological resource use, human intrusions and disturbance, residential and commercial development, and agriculture and aquaculture were the four main reasons for population decline and extirpation across the range and habitats of the species, with local differences in the level of exploitation (see Table 1, Supplementary Information).
documentation.habitats: The species is a generalist and opportunist and has adapted to living in a wide range of habitats, including forests, coasts, hills, and mountains (Fooden 1995). They occur in mangroves and swamp forests, particularly in riverine habitats; in lowland forests and in human-altered habitats, which include temples, roadsides, agricultural areas, and rural/urban settlements (Gumert 2011). Anthropogenic ecologies are an important aspect of their natural ecology (Fuentes et al. 2005, Gumert et al. 2011, Marty et al. 2020) and should be considered as such when considering their habitat types.
documentation.threats:
This species is threatened by habitat loss and degradation, human-wildlife conflicts, pet trade, subsistence hunting, and international trade for use in research (pharmaceutical and biomedical). Due to the combined impact of these threats, there has been an inferred decline in population numbers and area of occupancy over the past three generations. It is suspected that, as these threats have not been mitigated, this population decline and decline in area of occupancy will continue into the future.

Firstly, the species is threatened by habitat loss and degradation. The changing landscape of Southeast Asia is affecting Long-tailed Macaques by reducing available undisturbed habitat and increasing contact between M. fascicularis and humans (Gumert et al. 2011b). Deforestation and habitat fragmentation are widespread (Sodhi et al. 2004), and this impacts the kinds of habitats available to M. fascicularis. Environmental shifts are driving more of the M. fascicularis population into an extensive overlap with anthropogenic habitats (Gumert 2011). Furthermore, the synanthropic nature of the M. fascicularis relationship with humans leads to formal and informal population control measures, such as culling and sterilisation (Eudey 1994, Gumert 2004, Sha et al. 2009, PERHILITAN 2018, Hansen et al. 2021).

In relation to habitat loss: Mangroves are one of the preferred habitats of the Long-tailed Macaque, and it is in fact described as the ‘mangrove monkey’ in some regions, e.g., Thailand (Hamilton et al. 2022). Its delineated range encompasses 17,233 km² (21%) of the global mangrove forest (Hamilton et al. 2022). The destruction of coastal mangrove habitat due to shrimp culture has been recognized as one of the key factors for this species’ local extinction in Bangladesh (Hasan and Feeroz 2010, Kabir and Ahsan 2012, Ahmed et al. 2023). Crucially, mangroves have undergone rapid global declines due to degradation and deforestation, losing 20%–35% of their extent since 1980 (Polidoro et al. 2010). Between 2000 and 2016, approximately 3,363 km² of mangroves were lost (Goldberg et al. 2020). Notably, nearly 80% of the global human-driven loss occurred in only six nations: Indonesia, Myanmar, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand, and Viet Nam, all of which are range countries of the Long-tailed Macaque.

Secondly, the species is threatened by human-wildlife conflict. Macaca fascicularis is removed in large numbers in areas where it is perceived as a pest. For example, in Peninsular Malaysia, 493,823 individuals were removed over a seven-year period from 2011 to 2018 (PERHILITAN 2018). The Philippines has also experienced culling activities (GMA News 2022). This practice has contributed to known localised declines and extinctions and will likely contribute to population declines in the future.
Third, in some countries, the species is threatened by the pet trade. In Viet Nam, keeping the species as a pet is common, although the species is protected by law. Confiscated Long-tailed Macaques are often released without proper procedure, contributing to negative human-macaque interactions and possible disease and parasite introduction in the release area (Aldrich and Neale 2021).

Fourth, hunting for subsistence is also a threat to the species, mostly documented by anecdotal reports. In the Eastern Plains of Cambodia, however, hunting is monitored and well-documented (see e.g., Ibbett et al. 2021).

Lastly, the species is threatened by international trade (as described in other areas of this assessment).

In regard to habitat loss and the ability of this species to adapt to degraded habitats: Frequently, Long-tailed Macaques rely on edge habitats, comprising anthropogenic environments such as agricultural or rural areas that border natural forest habitats. While the Long-tailed Macaque may be able to live in forest edges and empty urban garbage bins, it is not able to fully adapt to living only in urban environments. Across the species' range, cities are expanding and forest cover is reducing (Global Forest Watch 2023). Between 2002 and 2022, the loss of tree cover was 52% in Cambodia, 18% in Indonesia, and 21% in Viet Nam (Global Forest Watch, 2023). In Indonesia, the urban population (% of total population) grew from 22% in 1980 to 58% in 2022 (The World Bank Group, 2024). As a result, the reduction of suitable habitats reduces the area of occupancy of the species even as the extent of occurrence remains large. The majority of M. fascicularis populations reside in unprotected areas, and there is extensive documentation of the challenges they face in these unprotected areas (as noted here and elsewhere in the assessment).
documentation.measures:
In general, there are only a few sustainable efforts to maintain Long-tailed Macaque populations in Southeast Asia. There is only one national-level program run by governmental wildlife agencies for censusing Long-tailed Macaques, and that is in Singapore (Sha et al. 2009, Riley et al. 2013). Establishing wildlife management programs for Long-tailed Macaques is critical, and urgent efforts are needed to establish regular censusing of M. fascicularis, as well as designing and implementing evidence-based management and protection plans throughout Southeast Asia.

It is also important to create coexistence programs for humans and Long-tailed Macaques led by local experts.

In terms of protection already conferred to M. fascicularis, the species is included in Appendix II of CITES, and thus is monitored and requires permits for international trade of live specimens and its parts, as well as quotas for wild off-take. In Cambodia and the Philippines, it is a normally protected species. In Myanmar, it has recently been assessed to be vulnerable, but legally is still a normally protected species. It is a protected species on Appendix 2B of Decree 84/2021/ND-CP in Viet Nam. It is not listed as a protected species in Indonesia (MOEF 2018), but any harvest from the wild can only be done as part of a quota, which for at least the last decade has been at or close to zero. In Thailand, it is not specifically listed on the Wild Animal Preservation and Protection Act, B.E. 2535 from 1992, but it is given the normal protection of wildlife, which restricts hunting and capture in all protected areas and forest lands. In Singapore, all wildlife is restricted from being captured, held as pets, or traded without permission, according to the Wildlife Act. In Malaysia, it is protected according to the Wildlife Conservation Act of 2010. In India, it is listed on Schedule I, Part I, Indian Wildlife (Protection Act) of 1972, and is considered an endangered species due to its limited range. In Lao PDR, it is listed as a management species, not a protected one.
documentation.use_trade:
As mentioned above, a workshop with Long-tailed Macaque experts (see Valle 2024 and Table 1, Supplementary Information) found that biological resource use is a main threat to Long-tailed Macaque populations, though this threat differs in severity according to the location.
 
The capture of free-ranging M. fascicularis occurs for both trade of specimens and subsistence across its range. In some locations, M. fascicularis faces threats from subsistence hunting, such as in Myanmar (San and Hamada 2011). Long-tailed Macaques are the most highly traded species of primate and are heavily demanded for biomedical and toxicology research (Cowlishaw and Dunbar 2000; Eudey 2008; Foley and Shepherd 2011; Hansen et al. 2021, 2022a; Gamalo and Ilham et al. 2023; Garber et al. 2024; Badihi et al. 2024). For many years now, large numbers of Long-tailed Macaques have been exported from Indonesia, Philippines, Cambodia, Lao PDR, Thailand, Myanmar, and Viet Nam; 163,780 individuals were traded from 2010 to 2019 in the legal international trade from these seven countries (Foley and Shepherd 2011; Hansen et al. 2021, 2022a; Gamalo and Ilham 2023; CITES 2024). The trade is even larger when non-habitat countries are included, such as China and Mauritius. Badihi et al. (2024), Garber et al. (2024) and Gamalo and Ilham et al. (2023) provide overviews of the source, purposes, and volume of this trade. According to CITES, most trade concerns captive-bred individuals (90%), however, this does not include supplementation of breeding stock by wild individuals.
 
It is noted that there can be a lack of sufficient scrutiny of this trade by wildlife managers, in order to ensure that capturing from the wild population is managed sustainably, or where not sustainable, that it is ceased. One issue arising in relation to the M. fascicularis trade, is the capture of macaques from the wild, which are then brought into breeding facilities in the eastern nations of Southeast Asia – Cambodia, Lao PDR and Viet Nam, (Lee 2011, Hamada et al. 2011). These wild-captured macaques are subsequently traded as if they are captive born and bred, thereby masking the true level of impact on the wild population (Foley and Shepherd 2011). From 2010 to 2019, 450,000 live Long-tailed Macaques were traded legally internationally, accounting for approximately 90% of the legal global primate trade that is monitored through CITES (Hansen et al. 2022a, Badihi et al. 2024). As the illegal trade (trade without CITES export permits) and the trade within habitat-countries is not included in CITES trade numbers, the illegal trade and the in-country trade is in addition to the numbers quantified from CITES export/import records.

The international trade of this species is coordinated by a few larger pharmaceutical companies with demand primarily coming from the USA, Japan, China and the EU, and most recently from Canada as well. China reduced exports greatly in 2019 (Warne et al. 2023, Kolby and Reaser 2024), which effectively changed the patterns of the international trade in Long-tailed Macaques, with habitat countries taking over as suppliers (Hansen et al. 2021, 2022a; CITES Trade Database 2022). For example, there was a notable increase in the export of Long-tailed Macaques from Cambodia between 2019-2020, rising from 13,922 to 29,466 individuals in just one year (Warne et al. 2023). Should China continue to not export Long-tailed Macaques, we expect habitat countries to continue to attempt to meet the international demand, which threatens the wild populations of the species (Badihi et al. 2024, Garber et al. 2024).

The international trade in Long-tailed Macaques is a multi-billion-dollar industry (Hansen et al. 2022a) with great fluctuations in price and export location (Gamalo and Ilham et al. 2023, Warne et al. 2023). According to CITES regulations, export countries must provide a Non-Detriment Finding report that contains information on the population sizes in the wild and in breeding centres to inform if the trade is sustainable or not. To date only Indonesia and China (a non-habitat country) have provided such a report (CITES 2024). It is pertinent for the conservation of the species that such reports are created, provided to CITES, and made publicly available.

The species is also threatened by national trade for pets and entertainment (Hansen et al. 2021, SMACC 2021) as well as trade in body parts (Chavez and Nijman 2024). The species is traded in markets for pets and entertainment, and online through social media. Numerous recent studies have documented the scale of this trade:
  1. The Social Media Animal Cruelty Coalition (SMACC) found 3,348 media posts depicting one or more Long-tailed Macaques in non-exhaustive online searches between September 2021 and January 2024. As no breeding of Long-tailed Macaques for pet trade or entertainment exists, all are believed to be wild-caught and the trade is believed to be greater than the results so far (Nicola O´Brien pers. comm. 2024).
  2. During past CITES meetings, information documents regarding the threats to the Long-tailed Macaque have been submitted by a cluster of NGOs (see for example, SSN, 2024). In February 2025, the CITES Animals Committee recommended all CITES parties suspend trade in Long-tailed Macaques with Cambodia based on documents provided by the US Fish and Wildlife Service and the Cambodian government. They also recommended that Viet Nam, the Philippines, and Cambodia remain under review of trade in Long-tailed Macaques reported as produced in captivity (CITES 2025). In 2025, another large report was released detailing illegalities in the trade in Long-tailed Macaques in and between numerous countries, albeit with anonymous authorship (Sandy River 2025).
  3. The increase in exploitation and wild capture during the pandemic is documented in a report about the unprotected macaques of Indonesia (MACC 2022). Prameswari et al. (2023) further supports this; from 2020–2022, both market and online trade saw an increase in Long-tailed Macaques offered for sale (with some fluctuation). More than 4,700 individual Long-tailed Macaques were offered for sale on Facebook in 2020 and 2021 in Indonesia alone (Prameswari et al. 2023). As no breeding centre claims to be selling Long-tailed Macaques privately within Indonesia, it is reasonable to assume that macaques offered for sale in these domestic/national markets are wild-caught. In total, 9,727 Long-tailed Macaques were detected for sale during the two years in Java and Sumatra, Indonesia.
  4. Nijman et al. (2017) focused on six animal markets in Java and Bali, Indonesia, and during 51 surveys 2012–2014) recorded 1,007 Long-tailed Macaques for sale. Morcatty et al. (2022) surveyed these six, and an additional seven, markets over the period 2016–2020 (179 surveys) and recorded 1,620 Long-tailed Macaques. This makes the Long-tailed Macaque the most common wild-caught mammal in these markets. Assuming that 60% of macaques are sold (or die) within a week, and with some 55 wildlife markets in Java and Bali (Nijman et al. 2017), this would suggest that 10,000–20,000 Long-tailed Macaques need to be extracted from the wild each year in order to meet the domestic demand for pets in this part of Indonesia alone.
  5. Chavez and Nijman (2024) surveyed wildlife trade shops in Bali, Indonesia, and 581 of the 754 primate skulls they recorded were from macaques, with traders indicating that most of these were Long-tailed Macaques. The trade of primate skulls in Bali was directed largely towards international tourists (Chavez and Nijman 2024).
  6. TRAFFIC (2023) has also documented the trade in the species.
documentation.rationale: The Long-tailed Macaque (Macaca fascicularis) has been assessed as Endangered under the A2cd, A3cd, and A4cd criteria, with Endangered being the lowest and highest plausible category. This is due to an inferred 50-70% decline over the past three generations (30 years) due to habitat loss and high levels of exploitation. In addition, as the threats facing the species and levels of exploitation have not been mitigated and are continuing at a similar pace, it is suspected that the species will continue to experience a population decline at a similar rate (50-70%) over the coming three generations (30 years), and therefore in addition over any three generation period including some past and some future years. This assessment is based on a range of data, both quantitative and qualitative, including historical and recent population estimates.
documentation.taxonomic_notes:
Macaca fascicularis is a wide-ranging macaque with a patchy distribution in South and Southeast Asia (Eudey 2008, Gumert, 2011). According to a variety of descriptions (Raffles 1821, Fooden 1995, 2006, Groves 2001), they are not distinguished by any distinct phenotypic features; however, they are one of the smaller macaques, and are named for their long tail, which approximates the length of their body and head combined. From a distance, the dorsal pelage is generally brown or greyish, with a whitish underbelly, as well as distinct black and white highlights around the crown and face. For example, their eyelids are often white, their crowns are bordered by white or black, and distinct white spots often occur on the skin in front of their ears. Closer inspection of the pelage reveals a mottled or speckled pattern, due to the individual hairs being of different colour. This hair patterning produces variation in shading between individuals and across populations. Hair shading includes yellowish, golden brown, reddish brown, brown, whitish, and blackened. Their skin coloration varies and includes white, pink, black, and brown tones. Under harsh sunlight, their facial skin easily tans. Adults are usually bearded on and around their face; however, around their snout and eyes, hair is short and sparse. Older females typically exhibit the fullest bearding, while for males, it is more whisker-like. They exhibit a lateral cheek crest that usually runs vertically along the face, but among some subspecific variations, the crest runs horizontally, bisecting the middle of the cheek. There are distinct differences in pelage colour between the different subspecies, ranging from almost black to light brown/grey.

The species is highly variable. Groves (2001) and Fooden (1995) have divided Macaca fascicularis into ten subspecies; however, as of recent, the most eastern subspecies, M. f. philippinensis has come under dispute (Smith et al. 2014). Consequently, it has been tentatively removed from the Red List assessment and is currently included with M. f. fascicularis. Along the northern part of their range, M. fascicularis regularly hybridizes with the Rhesus Macaque, M. mulatta (Fooden 1964). They have also long been known to hybridize with the Southern Pig-tailed Macaque, M. nemestrina (Bernstein 1966). Hybrids can also occur across subspecies (Bunlungsup et al. 2016, Gumert et al. 2019).

In regard to synonyms*: Simia aygula Linnaus 1758, Simia cynomolgus Schreber 1775, Simia fascicularis Raffles 1821, Macacus carbonaria Cuvier, 1825, Macaca irus Geoffroy 1826, Semnopithecus kra Lesson 1830, and numerous other names have been ascribed using the above genera, as well as genera assignments that have also included Macac, Pithecus, and Cynomolgus.

*There are numerous historical synonyms and mistaken names for this species. Early uses are highlighted here, but for a more complete historical listing and discussion, please refer to Napier and Groves (1983), Groves (2001), and Fooden (1995).
